awd_titl_txt: Collaborative Research: CIRC: Planning-C: Building a Safer Cyberspace by Creating a Centralized Research Infrastructure to Track and Mitigate Privacy Harms
awd_abstract_narration:
This project explores a proof-of-concept and feasibility evaluation to inform the future development of a centralized data repository to support the privacy research community. The repository will enable tracking and systematic study of privacy harms. Current incident reporting systems are designed to track the occurrence of large-scale data breaches, but there is currently no centralized reporting system to effectively track other types of privacy violations (e.g., online harassment, cyber abuse) that negatively impact end-users. Without access to this information, it is difficult to quantify / qualify how and to what extent different online platforms propagate privacy breaches, as well as how to redesign such systems to be more secure and trustworthy. 

Therefore, this planning effort aims to (1) solicit the opinions of privacy experts on the design of the repository; (2) prototype the repository and solicit feedback from experts piloting it; and (3) build on these learnings to develop a plan to develop a centralized privacy incident repository. This will ultimately enable researchers to work together to (1) identify and prioritize privacy harms and the factors associated with the incidents; (2) understand how various populations are impacted by these harms; and (3) develop and evaluate potential interventions. This repository is envisioned to support the protection of vulnerable end-users who are disproportionately threatened and harmed by digital privacy violations, addressing the recent R&D budget priority from the White House and the Office of Science and Technology Policy focused on reducing inequities. By identifying evolving privacy risks, we also work towards two other budget priorities -- advancing trustworthy AI technology and maintaining global security and stability.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project laid the foundation for a new research infrastructure to better understand and address online privacy harms. As digital technologies increasingly shape everyday life, individuals encounter a wide range of privacy violations; yet, there is no centralized system for collecting and analyzing these experiences. Our work addressed this gap by exploring how to design a shared repository of privacy incidents that supports research, informs policy, and ultimately contributes to a safer cyberspace.

A major outcome of this project was identifying the requirements for such a repository. Through interactive design workshops with computing researchers, we developed a prioritized set of use cases, identified the types of information (metadata) that should be collected, and examined potential risks to long-term sustainability. These activities revealed a clear priority: researchers most value privacy incidents reported directly by individuals, rather than relying only on sources like news reports or court cases. This insight shifted the direction of the project toward centering lived experiences.

To support this goal, we designed and tested a prototype interface that allows individuals to report their own privacy experiences. In a study with 160 U.S.-based participants, we examined what types of information people are willing to share and how they describe their experiences. We found that individuals do not naturally categorize privacy harms in the same ways researchers do, highlighting the need for translation between everyday language and academic frameworks. This led to the development of improved methods for collecting and classifying privacy incidents in ways that remain meaningful for both users and researchers.

In parallel, our research produced new scientific insights into the nature of privacy harms. Analyzing hundreds of user-reported incidents, we found that existing legal frameworks do not fully capture the range of harms people experience. Many harms are not immediate or tangible (such as financial loss), but instead involve ongoing psychological effects—such as anxiety, loss of trust in technology, and a diminished sense of safety. In fact, the most common harm reported was a loss of psychological safety, reflecting persistent concern about how personal information might be used in the future. These findings expand current theories of privacy by demonstrating that harms often accumulate over time and are shaped by social and technological contexts.

We also identified new patterns in how privacy incidents occur. Contrary to traditional assumptions that emphasize government surveillance, our findings show that corporations and interpersonal interactions are the most common sources of privacy violations. Incidents frequently involve data collection, targeted advertising, data sharing, or misuse of personal information, as well as actions by other individuals such as harassment or unauthorized sharing. Based on these findings, we developed an updated sociotechnical taxonomy of privacy incidents and harms that better reflects modern digital environments. This framework provides a common vocabulary that can be used by researchers, designers, and policymakers.

The project also advanced technical planning for a future large-scale system. We defined key features for the repository, outlined system architecture, and developed strategies for maintaining data quality and managing access. Importantly, we identified the need to balance accessibility with privacy protections—for example, limiting detailed data access to researchers while sharing aggregate insights more broadly.

Beyond technical and scientific contributions, the project strengthened the research community and supported workforce development. Graduate and undergraduate students gained hands-on experience in human-centered design, survey research, and data analysis, while also building professional networks through conferences and collaborative activities.

The broader impacts of this work extend beyond academia. By enabling systematic collection and analysis of privacy harms, the envisioned repository can inform public policy, support advocacy organizations, and empower individuals to share their experiences. Ultimately, this project contributes to a safer cyberspace by providing the tools and knowledge needed to better understand and respond to privacy challenges in today’s digital world.
